Premenstrual Syndrome and Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder

cycle timing · prospective ratings · mood and physical symptomsDo symptoms clear after menses, or persist through the cycle?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Before menses, then a symptom-free interval: suspect premenstrual syndrome (PMS) or premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD). Confirm with a daily symptom diary for at least 2 cycles before selecting treatment
  • PMDD: 5 or more symptoms, including a core mood symptom, with marked distress or impaired function; symptoms become minimal or absent after menses
  • Confirmed mild symptoms: exercise and stress reduction. Moderate or severe symptoms: a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI)
What it is

Recurrent menstrual-cycle symptoms affecting mood, the body, or both; PMDD is the more severe syndrome

Driver

Mechanism uncertain; heightened sensitivity to normal ovarian hormone fluctuations may disturb neurotransmitter signaling

Triggers

Reproductive years; family mood or premenstrual disorders; personal anxiety history

Chain

Proposed: luteal hormone sensitivity mood and bodily symptoms impaired daily function

Insights

Do normal hormone levels exclude PMS or PMDD? Normal hormone levels do not rule it out MechanismEstrogen and progesterone concentrations are normal; altered sensitivity, rather than excess hormone, is proposed

Does depression history explain a new cyclic complaint? A history of depression does not establish the cause of a new cyclic complaint Diagnostic distinctionChart the entire cycle to separate baseline mood symptoms from a distinct premenstrual syndrome

2Urgent risks
SafetyPremenstrual symptoms can include suicidal thinking

If suicidal thoughts are present, choose assess intent, risks and supports; make a safety plan.

3Differential
Look-alikes, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDurationDecides it
PMSFewer physical or emotional symptoms; functioning affected1 to 2 weeks before menses; recurrent over 3 cyclesSymptoms clear shortly after bleeding begins; a mood symptom is not required
PMDDProminent mood symptoms with more severe impairmentFinal premenstrual week; most cycles in the preceding yearAt least 5 symptoms including a core affective symptom; minimal or absent in the week after menses
Persistent depressed mood or loss of pleasureContinues across menstrual phasesNo postmenstrual remission of the ongoing depression
Premenstrual exacerbationA known mood, anxiety or other disorder worsens before mensesBaseline symptoms throughout the cycleThe underlying symptoms remain after menstruation starts
Physiologic premenstrual changesCyclic physical or mood changesBefore mensesDaily activities remain intact
Medication-induced mood symptomsNew symptoms after hormonal contraception startsBegins after the exposureImproves after the exogenous hormone is stopped
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext best step
Recurrent symptoms without a documented menstrual relationshipPMS/PMDD remains provisionalChart daily before starting a disorder-specific treatment
Mood symptoms remain after the periodPersistent mood symptoms or premenstrual exacerbationEvaluate the underlying disorder
Normal laboratory evaluationPMS/PMDD still possibleUse prospective timing and symptom ratings

Pause point. A familiar antidepressant is premature when the timing is still uncertain. Establish the cycle relationship first

5Diagnostic criteria
PMS Symptoms – 1 to 4 physical or emotional symptoms affecting function · Timing – recurring in 3 successive cycles; begin premenstrually and clear in the first days of bleeding
PMDD Count – At least 5 symptoms during the final premenstrual week in most cycles over the past year; at least one core mood symptom; marked distress or impaired function · Symptoms – Symptom setCore: mood lability, irritability/anger, depressed mood, or anxiety. Additional features: reduced interest or concentration, low energy, altered appetite or sleep, feeling overwhelmed, and bodily symptoms · Confirm – Improve soon after bleeding begins; minimal or absent in the postmenstrual week. Confirm daily ratings for at least 2 symptomatic cycles; exclude substances, medical causes and mere exacerbation of another disorder
6Severity
Function determines treatment
SeverityAction
Mild, confirmed symptomsLifestyle measures
Moderate or severe symptomsAdd pharmacotherapy; assess psychiatric comorbidity and safety
7Treatment
1

Firstconfirmed symptoms; mild impairment

Regular exercise and stress-reduction measures Symptom reliefA nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) or combined oral contraception may relieve physical symptoms and can be adjuncts in more severe disease; SSRIs target severe symptoms
2

Addmoderate or severe symptoms

An SSRI such as sertraline, fluoxetine or escitalopram
3

Raisesymptoms persist with the initial approach

Review response; another SSRI trial is reasonable before other drug classes
4

Adjunctlifestyle measures and multiple SSRI trials leave symptoms

Add cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT)
5

Contraceptioncontraception desired, or additional physical symptoms

Consider a combined oral contraceptive; significant mood symptoms warrant separate treatment
SSRI dosing choices
PatternRegimen
Unpredictable cycle or preference for daily dosingContinuous daily dosing
Predictable symptoms lasting over a week before mensesStart on cycle day 14; stop at menses or a few days afterward
A shorter predictable symptom intervalBegin with symptom onset; continue until a few days after menses
8Follow-up
Follow-up decisions
WhenDo
First treated cycleReassess symptoms and daily function; SSRI benefit may already appear
Persistent symptoms or lost symptom-free intervalReview the diary and reassess mood or anxiety comorbidity
Medication stoppedCounsel that symptoms commonly return
Practice
  1. 29-year-old with recurrent breast discomfort and irritability attends a routine visit Symptoms disappear between episodes; the patient has never tracked menstrual dates Examination is normal; work and relationships suffer during episodes → Daily menstrual symptom diary → Record symptoms and function through at least 2 cycles before selecting a treatment; recurrent symptoms alone do not establish menstrual timing
  2. A patient brings daily ratings recorded over three cycles Before each period, irritability, anxiety, sadness, overeating and fatigue disrupt work Symptoms are minimal after menses; this pattern occurred most months last year → Premenstrual dysphoric disorder → Five symptoms including core affective symptoms, impaired function and postmenstrual remission fit PMDD; ordinary changes preserve function and exacerbation leaves baseline symptoms
  3. A patient reports low mood and lost enjoyment throughout the month Symptoms worsen before each period but never disappear afterward A daily diary confirms ongoing depression with an additional increase in severity before bleeding → Premenstrual exacerbation → An existing mood syndrome persists across the cycle and worsens before menses; this is premenstrual exacerbation rather than an isolated luteal disorder
  4. A patient has prospectively confirmed premenstrual dysphoric disorder Severe irritability and anxiety disrupt employment despite regular exercise and stress reduction There is a clear symptom-free interval; contraception is not desired; cycles are unpredictable → Continuous daily sertraline → An SSRI is first-line pharmacotherapy for moderate or severe symptoms; continuous dosing suits unpredictable cycles, and contraception alone does not adequately target mood symptoms
  5. A patient brings a prospective diary confirming mild premenstrual syndrome Breast tenderness and fatigue recur before bleeding and clear afterward Symptoms briefly interfere with routine tasks; the patient wants the least intensive initial treatment → Exercise and stress reduction → Lifestyle measures are first-line for mild confirmed symptoms; drug therapy is reserved for greater symptom burden or a separate contraception goal
  6. A patient with premenstrual symptoms requests ovarian hormone testing Examination reveals no evidence of another medical disorder Symptoms recur before bleeding, but their severity and effect on function have not been recorded prospectively → Daily symptom and function ratings → Prospective ratings confirm timing and impairment; estrogen and progesterone levels are normal and are not diagnostic tests for PMS or PMDD
Pairs with Major Depressive Disorder: persistent depression across the cycle. Bipolar Disorder: ongoing mood episodes with possible premenstrual worsening. SSRI Adverse Effects: treatment tolerability.
Transferable rule

Record both the symptomatic phase and the interval between episodes before attributing symptoms to the menstrual cycle.
